$schema-note: WIN-271 (M4.5) mutation ledger. Every row was APPLIED to the named file in the working tree, the named command was run from the repository root, the file was restored, and the recorded exit code is what that run returned. `killedCase` is the FIRST case the run reported failing, read back out of the command's own output rather than predicted. Nothing here is a prediction.
tranche: M4.5 — channels behind a canonical ChannelRuntime port
purpose: A green suite proves the code passes its own cases. It does not prove the cases would notice if the property left. Each mutation removes exactly one property this tranche claims and records which named case turned red.
procedure: Read the file, replace one exact anchor (refused if it matches zero or more than one place), run the command with both streams redirected to a file, write the original back, read the log, record the exit code and the first failing case. For the two rows that mutate `packages/contexts/channels`, the command REBUILDS that package first and the driver rebuilds it again after restoring — the adapter consumes the context through its `dist/`, so a source mutation is otherwise invisible. The driver is `scripts/run-win271-mutations.mjs` and the rows it applies are `scripts/win271-mutation-plan.json`, both committed, so this sweep is re-runnable rather than described.

commands.slackAdmitBuilt: pnpm --filter @platos/context-channels build && pnpm --filter @platos/adapter-channel-slack exec vitest run src/signed-admission.test.ts
commands.channelsBuilt: pnpm --filter @platos/context-channels build && pnpm --filter @platos/context-channels exec vitest run

baseline.apps/core-api: 420/420 unit (integration excluded: no Docker on this machine)

mutations.name: M01 the replay window becomes one-sided
mutations.guards: a capture held and replayed with a FUTURE timestamp is refused too
mutations.why: Bounding only (now - t) leaves the other direction open: capture a signed request, present it with a timestamp far ahead, and 'too old' never fires. The window is |now - t| and this mutation makes it one-sided.
mutations.killedCase: a signature that does not verify is refused, with a code that says why > refuses STALE for a timestamp in the FUTURE, which is the same replay

mutations.name: M02 an unparseable timestamp is reported as INVALID rather than STALE
mutations.guards: the three inbound refusals stay three, because they are three operator actions
mutations.why: STALE says look at a clock and INVALID says look at a secret. Collapsing the unparseable case into INVALID sends an operator to rotate a secret that was never wrong.
mutations.killedCase: a signature that does not verify is refused, with a code that says why > refuses STALE for a timestamp that is not a number at all

mutations.name: M03 the structural staleness check is deleted and the vendor's is relied on
mutations.guards: STALE is decided HERE, so it cannot collapse into the SDK's single error class
mutations.why: The SDK signals absent, stale and invalid by throwing ONE class and separates them only by an English message. Deleting our own check makes a replayed request arrive as INVALID, which is the taxonomy hostage this adapter exists to avoid.
mutations.killedCase: a signature that does not verify is refused, with a code that says why > refuses STALE for a valid signature outside the replay window

mutations.name: M04 a present-but-empty signature header counts as signed
mutations.why: An empty header is not a signature. Accepting one would hand the request to the SDK with nothing to verify against, and what comes back is a vendor error rather than this adapter's own ABSENT.
mutations.killedCase: a signature that does not verify is refused, with a code that says why > refuses ABSENT for a header that is present and empty

mutations.name: M05 the bot's own message is admitted like any other
mutations.guards: an app must not run a turn on the message it just posted
mutations.why: Slack delivers the app's own post back to the app. Treating it as inbound starts a turn, whose reply is posted, which is delivered, which starts a turn: an unbounded loop costing a model call each time round and visible to the customer as the assistant talking to itself.
mutations.killedCase: the delivery that would loop forever > ignores the app's OWN message coming back

mutations.name: M06 a missing event id is synthesized from the message timestamp
mutations.guards: the admission key is the PROVIDER's own id and is never invented
mutations.why: The inbox is idempotent on [appId, eventId]. A synthesized key makes a redelivery unrecognisable, so one provider event can run two turns — and hashing the body instead would make a user who genuinely says the same thing twice get one answer.
mutations.killedCase: a message with nothing to deduplicate on is REFUSED, not ignored > refuses rather than admitting a row a redelivery could not collide with

mutations.name: M07 the thread key puts the channel in the wrong segment
mutations.guards: the DOMAIN's own reader recovers the channel this adapter wrote
mutations.why: `domain/inbound.ts::extractPlatformChannelId` takes the SECOND colon-separated segment and every `channel` routing rule matches on it. A key in any other shape makes those rules silently stop matching — no error anywhere, the rule simply never fires.
mutations.killedCase: a message becomes an InboundMessage > renders a thread key the DOMAIN can read the channel back out of

mutations.name: M08 a mid-flight timeout is classified UNAVAILABLE
mutations.guards: 'did not land' and 'do not know' are different facts with different remedies
mutations.why: UNAVAILABLE means retry me, nothing happened. A request that was WRITTEN and whose response was lost may well have posted the message, so retrying posts it twice into a customer's channel. This is the single most expensive misclassification the adapter can make.
mutations.killedCase: a delivery that times out mid-flight > is INDETERMINATE, and the far side really did receive the message

mutations.name: M09 an unrecognised throw defaults to UNAVAILABLE
mutations.guards: the classifier fails CLOSED on anything it does not understand
mutations.why: The commonest real instance is a proxy's non-JSON 502, where the request definitely left and the answer says nothing about whether the message was posted. Defaulting the unknown to RETRY is how the duplicate-message mistake gets made by a code path nobody reviewed.
mutations.killedCase: the provider's own refusals, in this context's vocabulary > maps a gateway's non-JSON error page to INDETERMINATE, not UNAVAILABLE

mutations.name: M10 the disposition table defaults OPEN
mutations.guards: a code the table has not been taught is RECONCILE, never RETRY
mutations.why: Defaulting to retry makes every future code silently repeatable, in the one direction that duplicates a customer-visible message. A repository failure surfacing through a delivery path would become a resend.
mutations.command: pnpm --filter @platos/context-channels build && pnpm --filter @platos/context-channels exec vitest run
mutations.killedCase: the default is CLOSED, and that direction is the whole point > sends an unrecognised code to reconcile rather than to retry

mutations.name: M11 the API base URL loses its trailing slash
mutations.guards: the vendor resolves a method as a RELATIVE REFERENCE against this constant
mutations.why: THE REAL DEFECT THIS TRANCHE SHIPPED AND CAUGHT. `new URL('chat.postMessage', 'https://slack.com/api')` is `https://slack.com/chat.postMessage` — the `/api` segment is dropped and every outbound call 404s against a path that has never existed. Asserting the constant would not see it; asserting the vendor's own resolution does.
mutations.killedCase: the ordinary path, so the failures below are not vacuous > resolves the API method against the base URL without eating a path segment

mutations.name: M12 the deadline timer is never cleared
mutations.guards: no per-call timer outlives its call
mutations.why: A timer left armed keeps the event loop alive, and a process that will not exit on SIGTERM because of one is a genuinely miserable thing to diagnose. The `finally` is what prevents it and nothing else does.
mutations.killedCase: a delivery that times out mid-flight > leaves no timer holding the event loop open

mutations.name: M13 a streaming edit becomes a second post
mutations.guards: streaming a turn back into a channel is an EDIT loop, not a message flood
mutations.why: `replacesProviderMessageId` is what makes a redelivered outbound event harmless — editing one message to the same text twice is indistinguishable from doing it once. Posting instead turns an at-least-once bus into a visible flood.
mutations.killedCase: streaming a turn back is an EDIT, not a flood > uses chat.update once a message id exists, so a redelivery is harmless

mutations.name: M14 an ignorable delivery is admitted to the inbox
mutations.guards: a verified event with no behaviour is acknowledged, never queued
mutations.why: Admitting reactions, joins and edits fills the inbox with rows no turn will ever run, makes the retry cap meaningless, and spends a lease on each.
mutations.command: pnpm --filter @platos/context-channels build && pnpm --filter @platos/adapter-channel-slack exec vitest run src/signed-admission.test.ts
mutations.killedCase: a handshake and an ignorable delivery are acknowledged, not admitted > drops the app's own message rather than filling the inbox with a loop

mutations.name: M15 a redelivery is reported as a first delivery
mutations.guards: the transport can tell a redelivery from a first delivery
mutations.why: `duplicate` is what lets a transport answer 2xx to a redelivery while knowing no new turn was queued. Reporting every admission as new makes a redelivered event look like a second message.
mutations.command: pnpm --filter @platos/context-channels build && pnpm --filter @platos/adapter-channel-slack exec vitest run src/signed-admission.test.ts
mutations.killedCase: a webhook that arrives twice > is admitted ONCE and acknowledged BOTH times

mutations.name: M16 one character of the PUBLISHED vector is mistyped
mutations.guards: the external anchor is the vendor's own published vector and not a local invention
mutations.why: If a character of the transcribed body were wrong, every signature case would still pass — they would simply be testing a different, self-consistent vector this repository made up. Only the independent `node:crypto` re-derivation against the published digest notices.
mutations.killedCase: Slack's own published request-verification vector > reproduces byte-for-byte under node:crypto, so the vector is the vector

mutations.name: M17 the upgrade differential compares the shipped line with itself
mutations.guards: the two lines under comparison are two independently published artifacts
mutations.why: If the audited alias ever resolved to the same install as the primary dependency, every case in the differential would compare a function with itself and pass forever — a green suite proving nothing about the 4.34 -> 4.40 move.
mutations.killedCase: the differential is not vacuous > is running two DIFFERENT artifacts

mutations.name: M18 the far side records a request only when it answers one
mutations.guards: what the far side RECEIVED is independent of whether it replied
mutations.why: The whole instrument. If `received` were appended only on the answering path, the timeout cases could no longer ask 'the adapter reported a failure — did the message actually land?', and every one of them would go quietly green against a server that had the message in hand.
mutations.killedCase: a delivery that times out mid-flight > is INDETERMINATE, and the far side really did receive the message

mutations.name: M19 the directory stays on UNIMPLEMENTED_ADAPTERS after gaining a constructor
mutations.guards: rule (C7) joins the unimplemented list to the adapter packages' own source
mutations.why: A readiness endpoint that says 'this directory is a generated interface' about a directory that has a working constructor is lying to an operator about why their channel is not serving. C7 reads the list back and joins it to the filesystem in BOTH directions.
mutations.killedCase: UNIMPLEMENTED_ADAPTERS says channel-slack cannot be constructed, but packages/adapters/channel-slack/src/index.ts exports a constructor; drop it from the list

controls.name: C1 the unmutated tree, before and after the sweep
controls.what: No mutation. The adapter suite is run unchanged, and `git status --porcelain` is checked clean afterwards, so no row's restore was partial and no kill above was inherited from the row before it.
controls.command: pnpm --filter @platos/adapter-channel-slack exec vitest run && git status --porcelain
controls.outcome: green and clean, as a control must be

controls.name: C2 THE DRIVER ITSELF WAS WRONG THREE TIMES, and each wrong version was believed for one run
controls.what: Not a mutation of the tree — a record of how this ledger was nearly a fiction, because the same three mistakes are available to the next person who writes one. (1) The first driver ran `cmd | tail -40` through `execSync`, which reports TAIL's exit status: it recorded 0/19 KILLED, every row a survivor, and the number was so obviously wrong that it was caught. (2) The second recorded 17/19 with M14 and M15 as survivors — both mutate `packages/contexts/channels`, which the adapter consumes through its `dist/`, so they were mutating a file nothing under test was reading. That is the failure mode a plausible-looking survivor count hides. (3) The third recorded 19/19 but with NO case name on any row, because the failing-case pattern was written against ANSI-coloured bytes and pnpm does not hand a child's output back on `execSync`'s error object. A ledger that says a mutation killed without saying WHAT noticed is the weakest possible form of this evidence.
controls.outcome: recorded, because a driver that is wrong in the SURVIVING direction is indistinguishable from good news
